summary:
Visitors in Moscow stand under the national framework of the Russian Federation. The July 2023 federal law bans gender transition outright, prohibiting both gender-affirming surgery and any legal gender recognition on official documents. The Supreme Court's November 2023 ruling designating the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation took effect on the state's unified list of terrorist and extremist organisations on 22 March 2024, and the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that "justifies" gender transition. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation.

Moscow is where this framework is enforced most visibly. The Moscow Times' survey of persecution in Russia during 2025, published 23 June 2025 and framed around arrests, club raids and extremism charges, records that Kotov, the first person charged with creating an extremist organisation on LGBT grounds, was arrested in Moscow in late December 2024.

The same reporting line covers Russia's first prison sentence under the LGBT-extremism designation, reported by the Moscow Times in February 2025. The case concerned organising activity and followed a court ruling in Siberia reported in January 2025, indicating that convictions under the designation have moved from administrative charges to custodial sentences.

Since the March 2024 addition to the unified extremist list, the designation has been used to arrest gay bar owners and to charge people for displaying rainbow-flag symbols. A visitor to Moscow should expect venue raids, identity checks and symbol-based charges to be live risks rather than residual ones.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement intensity in Moscow exceeds that of most other Russian cities, while the severity of the law itself is uniform nationwide. The federal anti-LGBT framework applies identically in the capital and in regional centres; what differs is police density, the frequency of venue raids and the visibility of extremism charges.

The trajectory of the case law runs upward. Charges under the extremist designation progressed from arrests in late 2024 to the country's first prison sentence in February 2025, and the organising charge underlying that sentence originated in a Siberian ruling reported in January 2025.

Public assembly has been closed to LGBT organisers in Moscow without exception. Moscow authorities have never approved a request to hold a gay pride rally, so a visitor should not expect lawful sanctioned visibility in public space.
localsOnly:
Residents of Moscow are subject to the same July 2023 prohibition on legal gender recognition as visitors, with no route to amend gender markers on Russian documents. Gender-affirming surgical care is banned nationally.

Same-sex marriage is not available in Moscow. In 2011 the head of the Moscow Registry Office stated publicly that attempts by same-sex couples to marry in Moscow are "doomed to fail", and no approval of such marriages has been recorded since.

Displaying rainbow-flag symbols and owning or operating an LGBT venue expose Moscow residents to extremism charges, as documented by the arrests of gay bar owners following the March 2024 listing.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of Kotov's case after his late December 2024 arrest in Moscow is not sourced in the inventory; the record establishes the arrest and the charge, not the verdict or sentence.

The number of extremism charges brought in Moscow specifically, as distinct from nationally, is not sourced here. Human Rights Watch's count of 101 extremism-related convictions as of 30 June 2025 covers Russia as a whole.

The 2011 statement by the head of the Moscow Registry Office is dated evidence of official hostility; current registry practice on same-sex marriage applications in Moscow is not separately sourced.

Whether any exception exists for visitors who have already changed gender markers abroad, and how Russian border and document checks treat foreign passports with amended markers, is not addressed by the available sources.
